authors: Dingel, Jonathan I.; Neiman, Brent
title: How many jobs can be done at home?
notes: Article number 104235 (no page range). Earlier version: NBER Working Paper 26948 (2020).
about: Classifies the feasibility of working from home for each occupation using O*NET task descriptions and merges this with occupational employment counts. Estimates that about 37 percent of U.S. jobs can be performed entirely at home, with these jobs paying more than average and varying widely across cities and industries.

authors: Barrero, Jose Maria; Bloom, Nicholas; Davis, Steven J.
title: Why Working from Home Will Stick
notes: Working paper (No. 28731, April 2021); not peer reviewed in this version.
about: Uses repeated surveys of more than 30,000 Americans (the Survey of Working Arrangements and Attitudes) to project that about 20 percent of full workdays will be supplied from home after the pandemic, versus about 5 percent before. Identifies drivers of persistence such as better-than-expected experiences, new investments and reduced stigma, and predicts lower spending in major city centres.

authors: Barrero, Jose Maria; Bloom, Nicholas; Davis, Steven J.
title: The Evolution of Work from Home
notes: Earlier version: IZA Discussion Paper 16436 (2023).
about: Documents that roughly 28 percent of paid workdays among U.S. workers aged 20-64 were done from home in mid-2023, about four times the 2019 level. Discusses why the shift has persisted, how it varies by worker and place characteristics, and its implications for pay, productivity and innovation.

authors: Bloom, Nicholas; Liang, James; Roberts, John; Ying, Zhichun Jenny
title: Does Working from Home Work? Evidence from a Chinese Experiment
about: Reports a randomized experiment at a large Chinese travel agency (Ctrip) in which call-centre volunteers were assigned to work from home or in the office. Home working raised performance by about 13 percent and reduced attrition, but home workers were less likely to be promoted conditional on performance.

authors: Brynjolfsson, Erik; Horton, John J.; Ozimek, Adam; Rock, Daniel; Sharma, Garima; TuYe, Hong-Yi
title: COVID-19 and Remote Work: An Early Look at US Data
notes: Working paper (No. 27344, June 2020); no journal version found. Survey shares differ between the June 2020 and later revisions.
about: Uses a nationally representative online survey fielded in spring 2020 to measure the rapid shift to remote work during COVID-19. Finds that about half of previously employed workers were working from home, with a large share having switched from commuting, and that the shift was larger in states with more remote-capable occupations.

authors: Mongey, Simon; Pilossoph, Laura; Weinberg, Alex
title: Which workers bear the burden of social distancing?
notes: Earlier version: NBER Working Paper 27085 (2020).
about: Builds occupation-level measures of work-from-home feasibility and of physical proximity at work from O*NET and validates them with time-use data. Shows that workers in low-WFH, high-proximity jobs are less educated, lower paid, hold fewer liquid assets and are more likely to rent, and suffered larger employment declines in the pandemic.

authors: Althoff, Lukas; Eckert, Fabian; Ganapati, Sharat; Walsh, Conor
title: The Geography of Remote Work
notes: Article number 103770 (no page range). Earlier version: NBER Working Paper 29181 (2021).
about: Shows that denser U.S. cities specialise in high-skill service jobs that can be done remotely. When these workers went remote during the pandemic, their spending on local consumer services fell, so low-skill service workers in big cities bore much of the economic impact.

authors: Gupta, Arpit; Mittal, Vrinda; Peeters, Jonas; Van Nieuwerburgh, Stijn
title: Flattening the curve: Pandemic-Induced revaluation of urban real estate
notes: Earlier version: NBER Working Paper 28675 (2021).
about: Documents that after the onset of COVID-19 house prices and rents fell in city centres and rose farther out, flattening the bid-rent curve in most large U.S. metros. The flattening was greater where working from home was more prevalent and housing supply less elastic.

authors: Ramani, Arjun; Bloom, Nicholas
title: The Donut Effect of COVID-19 on Cities
notes: Working paper (No. 28876, May 2021; revised December 2022). Title on NBER page is styled 'Covid-19'.
about: Uses U.S. Postal Service change-of-address data and Zillow prices and rents to show that population, business activity and real estate demand moved from dense city centres toward suburbs within large metros after 2020. Attributes this 'donut effect' largely to hybrid work, which keeps workers within commuting range.

authors: Delventhal, Matthew J.; Kwon, Eunjee; Parkhomenko, Andrii
title: JUE Insight: How do cities change when we work from home?
notes: Article number 103331 (no page range). Author order varies across listings; RePEc lists Delventhal, Kwon, Parkhomenko.
about: Uses a quantitative spatial model of the Los Angeles metropolitan area with agglomeration externalities and endogenous congestion to simulate a permanent rise in telecommuting. Predicts that jobs concentrate in the core while residents move to the periphery, commuting times fall, and core real estate prices decline relative to the periphery.

authors: Tolbert, Charles M.; Sizer, Molly
title: U.S. Commuting Zones and Labor Market Areas: A 1990 Update
publisher: Economic Research Service, U.S. Department of Agriculture
notes: Staff Paper No. AGES-9614, September 1996.
about: Uses 1990 Census journey-to-work data and hierarchical cluster analysis of county-to-county commuting flows to group all U.S. counties into 741 commuting zones. These zones are the standard definition of local labour markets in much U.S. empirical work.

authors: Fowler, Christopher S.; Rhubart, Danielle C.; Jensen, Leif
title: Reassessing and Revising Commuting Zones for 2010: History, Assessment, and Updates for U.S. 'Labor-Sheds' 1990-2010
about: Replicates and evaluates the original commuting-zone delineations and produces new 2010 zones and revised 1990 and 2000 zones using a consistent, purely algorithmic cluster method on census and ACS commuting flows. Discusses the sensitivity of commuting zones to methodological choices.

authors: Autor, David H.; Dorn, David; Hanson, Gordon H.
title: The China Syndrome: Local Labor Market Effects of Import Competition in the United States
about: Measures each commuting zone's exposure to rising Chinese imports from 1990 to 2007 through its initial industry mix, instrumenting with Chinese imports to other high-income countries. Finds that more exposed local labour markets experienced higher unemployment, lower participation, lower wages and larger increases in transfer payments.

authors: Autor, David H.; Dorn, David
title: The Growth of Low-Skill Service Jobs and the Polarization of the US Labor Market
about: Links the rise of low-skill service occupations and job polarization to falling costs of automating routine tasks. Using commuting zones as local labour markets, shows that areas initially specialised in routine work saw greater computer adoption, reallocation of low-skill workers into services and polarization of wages and employment.

authors: Moretti, Enrico
title: Local Multipliers
notes: Some secondary sources cite pages 1-7 from the author's preprint; the AEA page gives 373-77.
about: Estimates long-run local employment multipliers across U.S. cities: each additional tradable (manufacturing) job generates about 1.6 additional nontradable jobs in the same city. Provides a framework for how local demand shocks spill over into local services.

authors: Moretti, Enrico
title: The New Geography of Jobs
notes: ISBN 9780547750118 (hardcover). Place of publication: Boston/New York.
about: Argues for a growing divergence among U.S. cities driven by concentration of innovation-sector employment in a few hubs. Emphasises that high-skill jobs generate local multiplier effects on service employment and wages for less-skilled workers in the same city.

authors: Glaeser, Edward L.; Mare, David C.
title: Cities and Skills
notes: Second author's surname is properly spelled Maré.
about: Examines the urban wage premium and finds that much of it accrues over time rather than immediately on arrival. Interprets this as evidence that cities speed up the accumulation of human capital, consistent with learning-based agglomeration economies.

authors: Duranton, Gilles; Puga, Diego
title: Micro-foundations of urban agglomeration economies
container: Handbook of Regional and Urban Economics, Vol. 4: Cities and Geography (eds. J. Vernon Henderson and Jacques-François Thisse)
notes: Book chapter (chapter 48). Kind set to 'book' as the closest available category. UNCONFIRMED: chapter DOI not checked, left blank. Earlier version: NBER Working Paper 9931 (2003).
about: Organises theoretical micro-foundations of urban agglomeration economies into three mechanisms: sharing, matching and learning. Develops core models for each and compares their aggregate and welfare implications.

authors: Rosenthal, Stuart S.; Strange, William C.
title: Evidence on the nature and sources of agglomeration economies
container: Handbook of Regional and Urban Economics, Vol. 4: Cities and Geography (eds. J. Vernon Henderson and Jacques-François Thisse)
notes: Book chapter (chapter 49). Kind set to 'book' as the closest available category. Some sources date the handbook to 2003; 2004 used here.
about: Surveys empirical evidence on agglomeration economies, showing that they operate across industrial, geographic and temporal scope and attenuate with distance. Reviews evidence on Marshallian sources such as labour pooling, input sharing and knowledge spillovers.

authors: Combes, Pierre-Philippe; Duranton, Gilles; Gobillon, Laurent; Puga, Diego; Roux, Sébastien
title: The Productivity Advantages of Large Cities: Distinguishing Agglomeration From Firm Selection
about: Nests a firm-selection model and an agglomeration model and shows that selection left-truncates the productivity distribution while agglomeration shifts and dilates it. Using French establishment data and a quantile approach, finds that productivity advantages of large cities are explained mainly by agglomeration rather than firm selection.

authors: Callaway, Brantly; Sant'Anna, Pedro H. C.
title: Difference-in-Differences with multiple time periods
notes: Implemented in the R package 'did'. Earlier version: arXiv 1803.09015.
about: Develops difference-in-differences methods for settings with multiple periods, staggered treatment timing and parallel trends that hold conditional on covariates. Identifies group-time average treatment effects ATT(g,t) and proposes aggregation schemes (including event-study summaries) with bootstrap-based simultaneous inference.

authors: Sun, Liyang; Abraham, Sarah
title: Estimating dynamic treatment effects in event studies with heterogeneous treatment effects
notes: Earlier version: arXiv 1804.05785.
about: Shows that in two-way fixed effects event-study regressions with heterogeneous effects across treatment cohorts, the coefficient on a given lead or lag can be contaminated by effects from other periods, so apparent pre-trends can arise purely from heterogeneity. Proposes an interaction-weighted estimator that recovers convex averages of cohort-specific effects.

authors: Goodman-Bacon, Andrew
title: Difference-in-differences with variation in treatment timing
notes: Earlier version: NBER Working Paper 25018 (2018).
about: Shows that the two-way fixed effects difference-in-differences estimator with staggered timing equals a variance-weighted average of all possible two-group, two-period comparisons, including comparisons that use already-treated units as controls. Implies that the estimate is biased when treatment effects change over time, and provides a diagnostic decomposition.

authors: de Chaisemartin, Clément; D'Haultfœuille, Xavier
title: Two-Way Fixed Effects Estimators with Heterogeneous Treatment Effects
notes: Earlier version: NBER Working Paper 25904 (2019).
about: Shows that two-way fixed effects regressions estimate weighted sums of group-by-period average treatment effects in which some weights may be negative, so the coefficient can even have the wrong sign. Proposes an alternative estimator robust to heterogeneous effects.

authors: Roth, Jonathan; Sant'Anna, Pedro H. C.; Bilinski, Alyssa; Poe, John
title: What's trending in difference-in-differences? A synthesis of the recent econometrics literature
notes: Earlier version: arXiv 2201.01194.
about: Reviews recent advances in difference-in-differences econometrics, organised around relaxations of the canonical two-group, two-period model: staggered treatment timing, potential violations of parallel trends, and alternative frameworks for inference. Provides practical recommendations and highlights open questions.

authors: Borusyak, Kirill; Jaravel, Xavier; Spiess, Jann
title: Revisiting Event-Study Designs: Robust and Efficient Estimation
notes: Earlier versions on SSRN (2016) and arXiv 2108.12419.
about: Shows that conventional regression-based event-study estimators are biased absent strong homogeneity restrictions, and derives an efficient estimator that takes an imputation form: fit unit and period effects on untreated observations and impute counterfactual outcomes. The method accommodates time-varying controls and triple-difference designs.

authors: Rambachan, Ashesh; Roth, Jonathan
title: A More Credible Approach to Parallel Trends
notes: Earlier versions titled 'An Honest Approach to Parallel Trends'.
about: Proposes sensitivity analysis for difference-in-differences and event studies that bounds how far post-treatment violations of parallel trends can differ from observed pre-treatment trends. Yields partial identification and uniformly valid confidence sets under these restrictions.

authors: Bertrand, Marianne; Duflo, Esther; Mullainathan, Sendhil
title: How Much Should We Trust Differences-in-Differences Estimates?
notes: DOI taken from the RePEc handle; consistent with QJE 2004 DOI format.
about: Uses placebo state laws in CPS wage data to show that serial correlation leads conventional difference-in-differences standard errors to badly overstate precision, rejecting true nulls in up to about 45 percent of cases. Evaluates remedies such as collapsing to pre/post periods and allowing an arbitrary within-state covariance structure.

authors: Cameron, A. Colin; Miller, Douglas L.
title: A Practitioner's Guide to Cluster-Robust Inference
about: Provides a practical guide to regression inference when errors are correlated within clusters, including state-year difference-in-differences designs. Covers cluster-robust variance estimation, fixed effects, few-cluster corrections such as the wild cluster bootstrap, and multiway clustering.

authors: Abadie, Alberto; Athey, Susan; Imbens, Guido W.; Wooldridge, Jeffrey M.
title: When Should You Adjust Standard Errors for Clustering?
notes: Earlier version: NBER Working Paper 24003 (2017).
about: Argues that clustering is a design question, motivated by clustered sampling or clustered treatment assignment, rather than merely by within-cluster correlation of residuals. Proposes variance estimators for cases where conventional cluster-robust standard errors are overly conservative.
